Environment facts:
- Pi binary: /usr/bin/pi -> /usr/lib/node_modules/pi/packages/coding-agent/dist/bundle/cli.js
- Pi's SDK package: /usr/lib/node_modules/pi/node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent (also /usr/lib/node_modules/pi/packages/coding-agent). Docs: /usr/lib/node_modules/pi/packages/coding-agent/docs/sdk.md and docs/extensions.md; examples in packages/coding-agent/examples/sdk/.
- SDK exports: createAgentSession({cwd, agentDir, resourceLoader, sessionManager, settingsManager, tools?, ...}), DefaultResourceLoader({cwd, agentDir, additionalExtensionPaths?, noExtensions?, ...}) with async reload() and getExtensions() (a LoadExtensionsResult, which includes load errors), SessionManager.inMemory(cwd), SettingsManager.inMemory(), getAgentDir(). AgentSession has getActiveToolNames(); check the .d.ts in dist/core for a way to list all registered tools (name, description, promptSnippet/promptGuidelines if available) and extension load errors/diagnostics. Project-local extensions live in <cwd>/.pi/extensions/*.ts and may require project trust; find the SDK way to trust/load them (read docs about project trust / DefaultResourceLoader options).
- Extensions are TypeScript and import "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent", "@earendil-works/pi-tui", "typebox"; Pi's loader maps these to its own copies.

- Input: `pi-ext-tools <project-dir> [-e <extension-file>]... [--no-global]` where --no-global avoids loading the user's global extensions from ~/.pi/agent (load only the project's .pi/extensions and any -e files) if the SDK allows it.

# Tool standards

Every tool in the tools repo meets these. They are what make a tool worth
finding again: the next agent reads the catalog line, runs `--help`, and
uses the tool without reading its source.

## Name

- The name says what the tool does in the domain: `json-extract`,
  `orders-repair`, `log-errors-by-host`. Not how it works (`jq-wrapper`),
  not when it was written (`fix-nov`), not who asked (`acme-script`).
- `toolsmith-repo` accepts lowercase letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`,
  starting with a letter or digit.
- No language suffix (`.py`, `.sh`). The tool is invoked by name, and a
  suffix becomes a lie the day the tool is rewritten in another language.

## The catalog header

One of the first five lines is the catalog header: a line comment in the
tool's own language, then `toolsmith-v1:`, then one line saying what the
tool does and when to use it. The catalog is generated from these lines,
so a tool without one is invisible to every other agent, and
`toolsmith-repo install` refuses it (exit 7).

The exact shape: optional leading spaces, then `#`, `//` or `--`, then
optional spaces, then `toolsmith-v1:`, then the purpose text. Only the
first five lines count. Keep the purpose to one line; it is the whole
catalog entry.

Shell, `#` (bash, sh):

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# toolsmith-v1: Pull fields out of JSON lines; use for trawling structured logs.
```

Python, `#`, with room for an encoding cookie:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
# toolsmith-v1: Group log lines by host and count errors; use to find a noisy host.
```

Node, `//` (Node rejects anything but a hashbang on line 1, so the header
goes on line 2 or later):

```js
#!/usr/bin/env node
// toolsmith-v1: Diff two package-lock.json files by package; use when reviewing dependency bumps.
```

Lua, `--` (only where `lua` is already installed; check with
`command -v lua`):

```lua
#!/usr/bin/env lua
-- toolsmith-v1: Convert a TSV file to a Markdown table; use for pasting data into docs.
```

Tools are text scripts. A language with no line comment, or a compiled
binary, can't carry the header and is out.

## Help text

- `--help` and `-h` print help to stdout and exit 0.
- The help says when to use the tool and why, before the flags. An agent
  reading only the help must be able to tell whether this is the right
  tool.
- It lists every flag and argument, gives at least one example
  invocation, and says plainly whether the tool changes, deletes, or sends
  anything.

## Parameterized and reusable

Write every tool for the next caller, not just this one. That holds for
project-scoped tools too: write `orders-repair --since <date> --dry-run`,
not `fix-acme-orders-nov`.

- Paths, dates, IDs, hostnames, URLs and thresholds are arguments or
  flags, with sensible defaults where one exists. Nothing from today's
  brief is hardcoded.
- Read from files named on the command line or from stdin; write to
  stdout unless the output is large (below).

## Errors

Errors are written for an agent reader: say what went wrong and what to
try, on stderr, and exit non-zero.

```
json-extract: no field 'user.id' in line 14 of app.log. Run with --list-fields to see what's there.
```

## Output and context

- Show what the caller needs and no more. An agent pays for every line
  of output in its context.
- Overflow goes to a file under `${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/toolsmith-$(id -u)/<tool>/`
  unless the caller passes `--out <path>`. The tool prints the path it
  wrote, so the caller can read the rest if it needs to. The UID keeps
  users apart on Linux, where `TMPDIR` is usually unset.
- A tool never drops files into the caller's current directory
  uninvited.

## Side effects and --dry-run

Anything that mutates, deletes, or sends implements `--dry-run`. With it,
the tool prints exactly what it would do and does none of it: no file
written, no row changed, no request sent.

Prove the dry-run before trusting it. A `--dry-run` flag written seconds
ago has never run, and trusting it against real data first is how an
untested guard sends a real email. So, in this order:

1. Build a fixture in a fresh temp directory of your own
   (`mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/toolsmith-$(id -u)/fixture.XXXXXX"`): a few
   sample files, a scratch SQLite database, a stub endpoint, whatever the
   tool acts on.
2. Run the tool with `--dry-run` against the fixture. Check that its
   output describes the change, that the fixture is byte-for-byte
   unchanged afterwards, and that nothing was sent.
3. Only then may you run `--dry-run` against the caller's real target.

Never run the mutating action itself on the caller's data. The caller
does that, after its own dry-run.

- Prefer one tool with options over near-duplicates. When a brief is
  close to an existing tool, extend that tool.
- Changes are additive by default. A renamed flag keeps the old name as
  an alias. Existing output formats stay the default; new formats go
  behind a flag.
- A breaking change is allowed, but name it in the reply's `note` and in
  the commit message. Other live sessions on this machine may be holding
  the old command line.

Your choice per tool, within the header rule. Shell for small glue,
Python for anything with real parsing.

- Each tool runs with what is already on the machine. Don't install
  packages and don't depend on anything outside the standard library.
- Before choosing Python, check that `python3 --version` works. On a
  fresh Mac, `python3` is a stub until the Command Line Tools are
  installed.

The toolsmith's final message is this block and nothing else, one field
per line, in this order. The caller acts on it without parsing prose.

```
tool: /abs/path/to/bin/name
catalog: <the tool's catalog line, for the caller to quote to the human>
status: new | changed | existing
mutates: yes | no
verified: ran example | dry-run only | help only
assumed: <any gap in the brief the toolsmith filled, or "nothing">
note: <optional: breaking change, repo created at X, fallback identity, etc.>
```

- `tool:` the absolute path of the installed tool in the tools repo. The
  caller runs it by this path. Never a staged copy under the temp
  directory.
- `catalog:` the tool's catalog line exactly as `toolsmith-repo install`
  printed it after `catalog=` (or as it appears in the catalog, for an
  existing tool).
- `status:` `new` for a tool that didn't exist, `changed` for an existing
  tool you edited, `existing` for a tool that already did the job
  unchanged.
- `mutates:` `yes` if the tool changes, deletes, or sends anything, even
  only with some flags. Then it has `--dry-run`.
- `verified:` the strongest check that ran.
  - `ran example`: you ran the brief's example invocation, which was
    read-only, against the caller's files, and it did the job.
  - `dry-run only`: the tool mutates; you proved `--dry-run` on a
    fixture, and perhaps dry-ran it against the real target. The
    mutating action itself never ran.
  - `help only`: only `--help` ran, because there was no example, or the
    example couldn't run safely or at all here. Say why under `note`.

  flag name, a default, an output format, the scope), so the caller can
  re-brief if a guess is wrong. `nothing` if the brief covered it all.
- `note:` leave the line out when there is nothing to say. Otherwise one
  line, with items separated by `; `. Always include:
  - every `note=` line `toolsmith-repo` printed (the tools repo was
    created at a path, a fallback git identity was set, and so on);
  - any breaking change, and the old command line it breaks;
  - any `adopted=` files that `install` committed alongside the tool;
  - the scope, if you put the tool in a project scope, or fell back to
    global because the caller isn't in a git repo.

most reasonable choice, named under `assumed`. When it genuinely cannot
proceed (the brief is mission work, a prerequisite is missing, the tools

```

```

```
note: created tools repo at /Users/me/.local/share/toolsmith/tools
```

pi-ext-tools - list what Pi extensions register, without calling a model.

When to use: you wrote or changed a Pi (earendil-works coding agent) extension
and want to know, without starting an interactive session or spending tokens,
whether it loads and which tools it registers (with descriptions, prompt
snippets/guidelines and whether each tool is active by default). It goes
through Pi's own SDK (DefaultResourceLoader + createAgentSession), so it
resolves imports of @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent, pi-tui and typebox the
way Pi does. It never calls session.prompt and needs no model or auth.

Usage:
  pi-ext-tools <project-dir> [-e <extension-file>]... [--no-global] [--sdk <dir>]

Arguments:
  <project-dir>          Project whose <dir>/.pi/extensions are loaded. It is
                         trusted for this process only (nothing is saved to
                         trust.json).
Options:
  -e, --extension <f>    Extra extension file/dir to load (repeatable).
  --no-global            Don't load extensions from ~/.pi/agent (auto-discovered
                         or configured in settings) nor built-in extensions, and
                         use in-memory settings. Loads only the project's
                         .pi/extensions entries (*.ts, *.js, <dir>/index.ts|js)
                         and the -e files.
  --sdk <dir>            Pi coding-agent package dir. Default: $PI_SDK, else
                         derived from the realpath of the 'pi' binary on PATH.
  -h, --help             Show this help.

Output (stdout, JSON):
  { extensions: [{path, error?}],
    tools: [{name, description, active, source?, promptSnippet?, promptGuidelines?}],
    errors: [...] }
  source is the extension path that registered the tool ("builtin" for core tools).
  Extension console output is redirected to stderr so stdout stays JSON.
Exit: 0 ok; 1 an extension failed to load (or session setup failed); 2 bad usage.

Side effects: none intended on the project. Uses an in-memory session (no
session file). Without --no-global, Pi may refresh packages configured in your
global settings, exactly as starting pi would.

Example:
  pi-ext-tools ./my-project --no-global
  pi-ext-tools . -e ./scratch/my-ext.ts --no-global
